A positive-pressure pressure-demand SCBA with at least 30-minute service life, or a pressure-demand full-facepiece air-line respirator with auxiliary self-contained air supply.

Example: Apply it when selecting work practices, training, or personal protection.

Reference: p. 692 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is an assigned protection factor (APF) used for?
Back:
To estimate the level of protection expected from a respirator class when properly selected and used.

Example: Apply it when selecting work practices, training, or personal protection.

Reference: pp. 688–692 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: How is maximum use concentration (MUC) calculated in the book?
Back:
MUC = exposure limit × APF, subject to the applicable constraints and IDLH limits.

Example: Apply it when selecting work practices, training, or personal protection.

Reference: p. 692 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the result for MUC for a TLV of 10 ppm and APF of 10?
Back:
MUC = 10 ppm × 10 = 100 ppm.

Example: Apply it when selecting work practices, training, or personal protection.

Reference: p. 692 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the purpose of fit testing?
Back:
To verify that a tight-fitting respirator facepiece seals adequately to the individual user's face.

Example: Apply it when selecting work practices, training, or personal protection.

Reference: pp. 696–700 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the industrial hygienist's central professional function?
Back:
Anticipate, recognize, evaluate, and control occupational health hazards.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 727–741 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What scientific areas commonly support IH practice?
Back:
Chemistry, physics, biology, engineering, toxicology, epidemiology/statistics, ergonomics, and related health sciences.

Example: Apply the concept to the physical or chemical conditions of a workplace task.

Reference: pp. 727–741 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why must an IH understand industrial processes?
Back:
Process knowledge is needed to anticipate sources, emission mechanisms, exposure scenarios, and feasible controls.

Example: Apply it when observing a process, task, or non-routine operation.

Reference: pp. 727–741 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is professional judgment in industrial hygiene?
Back:
The informed application of scientific evidence, measurement data, experience, standards, and uncertainty to occupational health decisions.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: pp. 727–741 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is a key communication responsibility of the IH?
Back:
Explain hazards, exposure findings, risks, limitations, and control recommendations to affected parties in understandable terms.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: pp. 727–741 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why does the IH need knowledge of sampling limitations?
Back:
A measured concentration is only meaningful when the sampling strategy, instrument, analytical method, and data quality support the conclusion.

Example: Apply it when planning or reviewing a personal air sample.

Reference: pp. 727–741 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the relationship between IH and safety practice?
Back:
They overlap substantially, and professionals in each area often apply principles from the other discipline.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 727–741 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is a major ethical responsibility of an IH?
Back:
Protect worker health and well-being and base professional judgment on recognized scientific principles.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 727–741 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why should IH recommendations consider feasibility?
Back:
Controls must be technically appropriate and implementable within the real process, workforce, and operating environment.

Example: Apply it when evaluating capture, airflow, or contaminant control at a workplace source.

Reference: pp. 727–741 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the value of continuing professional development?
Back:
It keeps the practitioner's technical knowledge current as hazards, standards, methods, and control technologies evolve.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 727–741 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the safety professional's principal focus?
Back:
Prevention and control of safety hazards, incidents, and associated losses through technical and organizational methods.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 743–763 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What disciplines support safety professional practice?
Back:
Engineering, physics, chemistry, statistics, mathematics, measurement/analysis, human behavior, motivation, and communication.

Example: Apply the concept to the physical or chemical conditions of a workplace task.

Reference: pp. 743–763 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why do safety and industrial hygiene functions overlap?
Back:
Both evaluate workplace hazards and develop controls, and many hazards have both safety and health consequences.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 743–763 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is a key difference between acute safety and chronic health hazards?
Back:
Safety hazards often produce immediate injury potential, while occupational health hazards may produce disease or impairment after repeated or prolonged exposure.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: pp. 743–763 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why is communication important to safety professionals?
Back:
Controls depend on workers and managers understanding hazards, expectations, procedures, and consequences.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: pp. 743–763 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What role can the safety professional play in incident investigation?
Back:
Identify causal factors and contributing conditions and recommend corrective actions to prevent recurrence.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 743–763 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the value of management involvement in safety and health?
Back:
Visible management commitment supports accountability, resources, participation, and implementation of controls.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 743–763 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why should safety and IH programs be coordinated?
Back:
Many hazards require integrated assessment and controls, and coordination avoids conflicting or duplicated efforts.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 743–763 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is an example of a shared control between safety and IH?
Back:
Machine/process enclosure, ventilation, isolation, training, PPE, or work-practice controls may address both safety and health hazards.

Example: Apply it when evaluating capture, airflow, or contaminant control at a workplace source.

Reference: pp. 743–763 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is a practical characteristic of an effective safety program?
Back:
Clear responsibilities, hazard identification, risk control, training, employee involvement, evaluation, and follow-up.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 743–763 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is occupational medicine?
Back:
A medical field focused on worker health in relation to work, including prevention, diagnosis, treatment, surveillance, and fitness for work.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 765–773 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why must occupational medicine work closely with industrial hygiene?
Back:
Medical findings and exposure information complement each other in recognizing work-related disease and preventing exposure.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 765–773 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the role of medical surveillance?
Back:
To identify health effects or early indicators associated with workplace hazards and help evaluate the effectiveness of preventive measures.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: pp. 765–773 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is fitness-for-duty assessment?
Back:
Evaluation of whether a worker's health status is compatible with the essential demands and hazards of a job.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: pp. 765–773 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why is exposure history important to occupational medicine?
Back:
It provides context for interpreting symptoms, test results, disease patterns, and possible work-related causation.

Example: Use it to interpret how a hazardous agent may affect a worker after exposure.

Reference: pp. 765–773 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is preplacement medical evaluation intended to accomplish?
Back:
Identify relevant health conditions and establish whether a worker can safely perform the job given its demands and hazards.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: pp. 765–773 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: How can medical findings support an IH program?
Back:
They can identify patterns suggesting inadequate control or previously unrecognized hazards, prompting further exposure evaluation.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 765–773 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why is confidentiality important in occupational medicine?
Back:
Personal medical information must be protected while communicating the information necessary for health and safety decisions.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 765–773 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the preventive emphasis of occupational medicine?
Back:
Prevent work-related disease and injury rather than relying solely on diagnosis and treatment after harm occurs.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 765–773 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why should medical and exposure data be interpreted together?
Back:
Health outcomes alone do not define exposure, and exposure measurements alone do not establish disease; the two streams provide complementary evidence.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: pp. 765–773 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is occupational health nursing focused on?
Back:
Promotion, protection, and restoration of worker health within the context of a safe and healthy work environment.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 775–791 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is a primary-prevention orientation in occupational health nursing?
Back:
Emphasis on preventing injury and illness before they occur through hazard control, health promotion, education, and surveillance.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 775–791 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is case management?
Back:
Coordinating care and return-to-work processes for workers who become injured or ill.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 775–791 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What health education functions can an occupational health nurse perform?
Back:
Counseling, health education, training, prevention programs, and worker communication.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: pp. 775–791 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why is the worksite important to occupational health nursing?
Back:
It provides the context in which work exposures, job demands, health status, and prevention opportunities interact.

Example: Apply it when observing a process, task, or non-routine operation.

Reference: pp. 775–791 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: How can OHNs contribute to exposure assessment?
Back:
They can provide clinical observations, worker histories, health trends, and information about symptoms associated with work tasks.

Example: Apply it when planning or reviewing a personal air sample.

Reference: pp. 775–791 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why is interdisciplinary cooperation important?
Back:
IH, nursing, medicine, safety, management, and employees contribute different information needed for comprehensive prevention.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 775–791 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is health promotion?
Back:
Efforts that support workers in improving and maintaining health, in addition to preventing occupational disease.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 775–791 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is secondary prevention?
Back:
Early detection and intervention to prevent progression of disease or impairment.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: pp. 775–791 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is tertiary prevention?
Back:
Management of established disease or impairment to reduce disability and restore function where possible.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: pp. 775–791 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the primary objective of an industrial hygiene program?
Back:
Prevention of occupational disease and injury through anticipation, recognition, evaluation, and control of health hazards.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: p. 793 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is workplace characterization?
Back:
Description of workplace processes and operations, emphasizing areas with potential exposure to environmental hazards.

Example: Apply it when planning or reviewing a personal air sample.

Reference: p. 796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is workforce characterization?
Back:
Grouping and description of employees with similar work duties or job classifications.

Example: Apply it when planning or reviewing a personal air sample.

Reference: p. 796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is agent characterization?
Back:
An inventory and description of environmental agents, including health effects, use, quantities, and physical properties.

Example: Apply it when planning or reviewing a personal air sample.

Reference: p. 796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which IH program element establishes health and safety policy?
Back:
Health and safety policy.

Example: A written policy defines the program’s scope and commitments.

Reference: p. 796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which IH program element assigns leadership duties and accountability?
Back:
Management responsibilities.

Example: A manager is assigned responsibility for correcting exposure-control deficiencies.

Reference: p. 796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which IH program element communicates chemical hazards to workers?
Back:
Hazard communication.

Example: Workers receive hazard information before using a new chemical.

Reference: p. 796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which IH program element governs approval of chemicals and equipment?
Back:
Chemical/equipment authorization.

Example: A new solvent is reviewed before being introduced to a process.

Reference: p. 796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which IH program element characterizes worker exposures?
Back:
Exposure assessment.

Example: Personal sampling is planned for a similar exposure group.

Reference: p. 796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which IH program element addresses capture and removal of airborne contaminants?
Back:
Ventilation.

Example: A hood is inspected to confirm it captures the contaminant.

Reference: p. 796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which IH program element addresses indoor environmental conditions?
Back:
Indoor air quality (IAQ).

Example: Investigate complaints associated with a building ventilation system.

Reference: p. 796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which IH program element evaluates ergonomic risk factors?
Back:
Ergonomics.

Example: Assess force, repetition, posture, and recovery time.

Reference: p. 796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which IH program element addresses ionizing or nonionizing sources?
Back:
Radiation safety.

Example: Assess exposure near an industrial radiography source.

Reference: p. 796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which IH program element addresses occupational sound exposure?
Back:
Hearing conservation.

Example: Monitor noise and track audiometric results.

Reference: p. 796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which IH program element addresses toxic gas hazards?
Back:
Toxic-gas hazard management.

Example: Assess a potential gas release and the need for detection or control.

Reference: p. 796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which IH program element addresses workplace biological agents?
Back:
Biohazard management.

Example: Evaluate aerosol and contact pathways during a biological task.

Reference: p. 796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which IH program element governs personal protective equipment?
Back:
PPE management.

Example: Select gloves based on chemical compatibility and breakthrough data.

Reference: p. 796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which IH program element prepares for unexpected harmful releases?
Back:
Emergency response.

Example: Plan for a loss of containment or an accidental release.

Reference: p. 796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which IH program activity checks conditions and program implementation?
Back:
Inspections and audits.

Example: Document a control deficiency and track corrective action.

Reference: p. 796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why is audit follow-up essential?
Back:
Without action plans, progress reports, or follow-up audits, much of the audit's value can be lost.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: p. 800 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What does effective training require?
Back:
A demonstrated need, clear measurable objectives, activities that build the desired skills/knowledge, participation and practice, evaluation, and revision when needed.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 798–799 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What was the main regulatory situation before 1970?
Back:
Occupational safety and health regulation was largely a state responsibility, with limited uniformity and enforcement.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: p. 807 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What federal law created OSHA?
Back:
The Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 (OSHAct).

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 807–810 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What broad authority does the OSHAct give the Secretary of Labor?
Back:
Authority to promulgate/modify/revoke standards, conduct inspections and investigations, issue citations and penalties, require records, address imminent danger, and oversee state plans.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: p. 808 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is a PEL?
Back:
A Permissible Exposure Limit established by OSHA and carrying the force of law.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: pp. 809–810 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is a NIOSH REL?
Back:
A Recommended Exposure Limit developed by NIOSH to guide occupational exposure control and OSHA rulemaking.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: pp. 809–810 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is an ACGIH TLV?
Back:
A health-based guideline published by ACGIH; the book emphasizes that TLVs are not mandatory OSHA standards.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: p. 24 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why should a hygienist distinguish PELs from TLVs?
Back:
They differ in legal status and development; a TLV is a voluntary professional guideline, whereas an OSHA PEL is a regulatory requirement.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: p. 24 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is an OSHA standard?
Back:
A legally enforceable occupational safety or health requirement promulgated under federal authority.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 807–823 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is an imminent danger concept?
Back:
A situation in which workplace conditions could reasonably be expected to cause death or serious physical harm before normal enforcement procedures could eliminate the danger.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 808–823 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why are recordkeeping requirements important?
Back:
They support regulatory compliance, program evaluation, trend analysis, and documentation of occupational injuries/illnesses and hazards.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 807–823 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: When was the Occupational Safety and Health Act adopted?
Back:
December 1970, according to the history presented in Chapter 29.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 825–827 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which federal agency administers and enforces OSHA standards?
Back:
The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA).

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 825–830 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What independent commission did the OSHAct establish to review OSHA contested cases?
Back:
The Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission (OSHRC).

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 900–901 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the basic purpose of OSHA's enforcement function?
Back:
To promote compliance with occupational safety and health requirements and protect workers through standards, inspections, citations, and related activities.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 825–892 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What was a major development in OSHA's noise regulation history described in the chapter?
Back:
The Hearing Conservation Amendment became effective in 1983 after extensive rulemaking and litigation.

Example: Use it when evaluating workplace noise exposure or a hearing-conservation program.

Reference: pp. 870–875 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is OSHA's relationship with state-plan states?
Back:
States may operate approved occupational safety and health programs under plans meeting federal requirements, subject to federal oversight.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 878–883 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What role did OSHA voluntary programs play in the history described?
Back:
They encouraged employer participation beyond enforcement, including consultation and Voluntary Protection Programs.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 874–875 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why is OSHA rulemaking history relevant to IH practice?
Back:
It explains how standards, enforcement policies, legal challenges, and regulatory decisions shape the requirements under which hygienists work.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 825–892 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is a key lesson from the chapter's history of litigation?
Back:
OSHA standards and enforcement have repeatedly been shaped by statutory interpretation, court decisions, stakeholder challenges, and administrative processes.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 850–892 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why should current OSHA requirements be checked rather than relying on this 2002 history alone?
Back:
Regulations and interpretations can change after publication; the chapter provides historical context, not a current regulatory database.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Reference: pp. 825–892 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the legal status of an ACGIH TLV according to this book?
Back:
It is a voluntary advisory guideline, not a mandatory federal or state employee-exposure standard.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: pp. 24, 919+ — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the purpose of TLVs according to the ACGIH description reproduced in the book?
Back:
They are guides intended to assist in controlling health hazards, not precise boundaries between safe and dangerous concentrations.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: p. 139 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is a BEI?
Back:
An ACGIH advisory biological limit value based on a determinant measured in biological media such as urine, blood, or expired air.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: p. 1004 (glossary) — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What can a BEI measure?
Back:
The substance itself, a metabolite, or another biological determinant associated with exposure.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: p. 1004 (glossary) — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is a key advantage of biological monitoring compared with air sampling?
Back:
Biological monitoring can provide information about absorbed dose from all exposure routes and physiological effects of the total absorbed dose.

Example: Apply it when planning or reviewing a personal air sample.

Reference: pp. 923–924 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: How long is the TLV-STEL averaging period?
Back:
15 minutes.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: p. 24 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: How often may exposures above the TLV-TWA but at or below the STEL occur?
Back:
No more than four times per workday, with at least 60 minutes between successive exposures in that range.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: p. 24 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is a ceiling limit intended to represent?
Back:
A concentration that should not be exceeded during any part of the working exposure.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: p. 24 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is At STP, what molar volume does the book use for an ideal gas?
Back:
22.4 L per gram-mole at 0°C and 760 mmHg.

Example: Apply the concept to the physical or chemical conditions of a workplace task.

Reference: p. 512 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is At 25°C and the same pressure, what molar volume does the book use?
Back:
24.45 L per gram-mole.

Example: Apply the concept to the physical or chemical conditions of a workplace task.

Reference: p. 512 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the relationship between ppm and volume fraction?
Back:
ppm is a volume-to-volume expression: parts of contaminant per million parts of air.

Example: Apply the concept to the physical or chemical conditions of a workplace task.

Reference: p. 512 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is 1% by volume in ppm?
Back:
10,000 ppm.

Example: Apply the concept to the physical or chemical conditions of a workplace task.

Reference: p. 157 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What gas-law relationship is used when temperature is constant?
Back:
P₁V₁ = P₂V₂; gas volume varies inversely with pressure at constant temperature.

Example: Apply the concept to the physical or chemical conditions of a workplace task.

Reference: p. 512 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What gas-law relationship applies at constant pressure?
Back:
Gas volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature (Kelvin or Rankine).

Example: Apply the concept to the physical or chemical conditions of a workplace task.

Reference: p. 512 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the rule for significant figures in addition/subtraction?
Back:
The result must not have more decimal places than the number with the fewest decimal places.

Example: Apply the concept to the physical or chemical conditions of a workplace task.

Reference: p. 995 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the rule for significant figures in multiplication/division?
Back:
The result must not have more significant digits than the factor with the fewest significant digits.

Example: Apply the concept to the physical or chemical conditions of a workplace task.

Reference: p. 995 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: How do you write 5,320,000 in scientific notation with three significant digits?
Back:
5.32 × 10⁶.

Example: Apply the concept to the physical or chemical conditions of a workplace task.

Reference: p. 995 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is a logarithm?
Back:
The exponent to which a selected base must be raised to produce a number: aˣ = y is equivalent to x = logₐ y.

Example: Apply the concept to the physical or chemical conditions of a workplace task.

Reference: p. 996 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the base of common logarithms?
Back:
10.

Example: Apply the concept to the physical or chemical conditions of a workplace task.

Reference: p. 996 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the base of natural logarithms?
Back:
e ≈ 2.71828.

Example: Apply the concept to the physical or chemical conditions of a workplace task.

Reference: p. 996 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the relationship between geometric mean and log-transformed data?
Back:
For lognormal data, the geometric mean is the antilog of the mean of the logarithmically transformed observations.

Example: Use it when interpreting variability or uncertainty in workplace measurements.

Reference: p. 997 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What does a GSD of 1.0 indicate?
Back:
No variability in the environmental measurements represented by the GSD.

Example: Use it when interpreting variability or uncertainty in workplace measurements.

Reference: p. 998 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What does a GSD of 2.0 or greater indicate?
Back:
Relatively high environmental variability.

Example: Use it when interpreting variability or uncertainty in workplace measurements.

Reference: p. 998 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: When should a lognormal distribution generally be assumed for occupational exposure data?
Back:
When multiple samples are used to characterize average employee exposure.

Example: Use it when interpreting variability or uncertainty in workplace measurements.

Reference: p. 997 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: When does the book say a normal distribution may be used for exposure evaluation?
Back:
For a ceiling check or when sampling covers the entire time period for which the standard is defined, so environmental time variability is represented in the sample.

Example: Use it when interpreting variability or uncertainty in workplace measurements.

Reference: p. 997 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the coefficient of variation (CV)?
Back:
A measure of relative variability, also called relative standard deviation.

Example: Use it when interpreting variability or uncertainty in workplace measurements.

Reference: p. 997 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: For a nonvarying property, what fraction falls within ±2 CV of the mean?
Back:
About 95%.

Example: Use it when interpreting variability or uncertainty in workplace measurements.

Reference: p. 997 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the dB equation used in the appendix example for relative loudness?
Back:
N₍dB₎ = 10 log₁₀(N₂/N₁).

Example: Use it when evaluating workplace noise exposure or a hearing-conservation program.

Reference: p. 996 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: A worker has 50 ppm exposure for 2 h and 0 ppm for 6 h. What is the 8-h TWA?
Back:
TWA = [(50×2)+(0×6)]/8 = 12.5 ppm.

Example: Apply it when planning or reviewing a personal air sample.

Reference: p. 514 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: A worker has 100 ppm exposure for 30 min in an 8-h shift and 0 ppm otherwise. What is the 8-h TWA?
Back:
TWA = 100×0.5/8 = 6.25 ppm.

Example: Apply it when planning or reviewing a personal air sample.

Reference: p. 514 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: A pump runs at 2.5 L/min for 480 min. What volume of air is sampled?
Back:
V = 2.5×480 = 1,200 L = 1.20 m³.

Example: Apply it when planning or reviewing a personal air sample.

Reference: p. 531 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: 6 mg collected from 1.20 m³ of air: what is the concentration?
Back:
C = 6 mg/1.20 m³ = 5.0 mg/m³.

Example: Apply it when planning or reviewing a personal air sample.

Reference: p. 523 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Is a fixed-location sample 20 ft from a worker automatically representative of personal exposure?
Back:
No. The book identifies personal sampling in the breathing zone as preferred because fixed-location conditions may differ from those experienced by the worker.

Example: Apply it when planning or reviewing a personal air sample.

Reference: p. 523 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Calibration error makes results consistently 15% high. Is this an accuracy or precision problem?
Back:
Accuracy. The systematic bias moves results away from the true value.

Example: Use it when interpreting variability or uncertainty in workplace measurements.

Reference: p. 510 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Repeated samples vary widely day to day. Is this random variability or systematic bias?
Back:
Random/environmental variability; it affects precision rather than creating a consistent bias.

Example: Use it when interpreting variability or uncertainty in workplace measurements.

Reference: pp. 510, 997 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: If a lognormal exposure distribution has GSD=1.0, what does that imply?
Back:
The book treats GSD=1.0 as no environmental variability.

Example: Use it when interpreting variability or uncertainty in workplace measurements.

Reference: p. 998 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What distribution is a reasonable starting assumption for positively skewed exposure data?
Back:
A lognormal distribution.

Example: Use it when interpreting variability or uncertainty in workplace measurements.

Reference: p. 995 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: TWA=8 ppm; TLV-TWA=10 ppm; 15-min result=15 ppm. What additional limit should be checked?
Back:
The applicable TLV-STEL or ceiling criterion; being below the TWA does not by itself rule out a short-term overexposure.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: p. 24 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why can an exposure below a TLV still warrant investigation?
Back:
TLVs are guides rather than absolute safe/unsafe boundaries, and individual susceptibility or other circumstances can warrant further evaluation.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: pp. 24, 139 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: A chemical has no OSHA PEL, NIOSH REL, or ACGIH TLV. What information sources can an IH use?
Back:
Internal exposure guidelines, toxicology data, literature, health surveys, manufacturer information, and other credible sources; the book emphasizes using the best available information.

Example: Apply it when interpreting exposure criteria and communicating chemical hazards.

Reference: p. 488 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: A large compressed-gas dense-vapor leak occurs. Could a floor-level hood help?
Back:
Yes, a substantial dense-gas/vapor release can form a ground-hugging plume, making low-level capture potentially advantageous.

Example: Apply it when evaluating capture, airflow, or contaminant control at a workplace source.

Reference: p. 620 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: At 1,000 ppm, should a dense solvent vapor be assumed to stay at floor level?
Back:
No. At such dilute concentrations, the vapor-air mixture density is close to that of air and random air currents can disperse it.

Example: Apply it when evaluating capture, airflow, or contaminant control at a workplace source.

Reference: p. 620 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Dust capture fails when the worker stands between source and hood. Which hood principle is violated?
Back:
The hood should be positioned so the contaminant is moved away from the operator's breathing zone before capture.

Example: Apply it when evaluating capture, airflow, or contaminant control at a workplace source.

Reference: p. 595 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why is a close-fitting hood attractive for dusty portable-tool operations?
Back:
It can achieve high capture velocity with relatively low exhaust volume, reducing the airflow requirement.

Example: Apply it when evaluating capture, airflow, or contaminant control at a workplace source.

Reference: p. 596 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Dust settles in an LEV duct at 1,000 fpm. What design issue should be investigated?
Back:
Insufficient transport velocity; the book cites roughly 3,000–4,000 ft/min as a common minimum range for ordinary dusts.

Example: Apply it when evaluating capture, airflow, or contaminant control at a workplace source.

Reference: p. 624 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: At constant flow, what happens to average velocity when LEV duct diameter decreases?
Back:
It increases because the same airflow passes through a smaller cross-sectional area.

Example: Apply it when evaluating capture, airflow, or contaminant control at a workplace source.

Reference: pp. 623–624 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: At constant flow, what happens to pressure loss when duct diameter decreases?
Back:
It increases because the higher velocity produces greater friction and pressure losses, potentially increasing fan power requirements.

Example: Apply it when evaluating capture, airflow, or contaminant control at a workplace source.

Reference: p. 624 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: A continuous source affects few nearby workers. Which ventilation approach is favored?
Back:
Local exhaust ventilation, because it captures the contaminant at the source and generally needs less airflow than dilution.

Example: Apply it when evaluating capture, airflow, or contaminant control at a workplace source.

Reference: p. 595 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: After a spill, room concentration is 4,000 ppm. If Q′ doubles, what happens to purge time?
Back:
It is approximately halved, because t is proportional to 1/Q′ in the exponential purging relationship.

Example: Apply it when evaluating capture, airflow, or contaminant control at a workplace source.

Reference: p. 634 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: In the dilution equation, what happens to required Q when target concentration L is halved?
Back:
Q doubles, because Q is inversely proportional to L.

Example: Apply it when evaluating capture, airflow, or contaminant control at a workplace source.

Reference: p. 633 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: For the book's dilution equation, if the safety factor K rises from 3 to 6, what happens to Q?
Back:
Q doubles, because Q is directly proportional to K.

Example: Apply it when evaluating capture, airflow, or contaminant control at a workplace source.

Reference: p. 633 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: If an indoor WBGT is calculated from Tnwb=20°C and Tgt=30°C, what is WBGTin?
Back:
0.7(20)+0.3(30)=14+9=23°C.

Example: Apply it when evaluating a hot-work task, clothing, and workload.

Reference: p. 329 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: If outdoor WBGT uses Tnwb=25°C, Tgt=35°C, and Tdb=30°C, what is WBGTout?
Back:
0.7(25)+0.2(35)+0.1(30)=17.5+7+3=27.5°C.

Example: Apply it when evaluating a hot-work task, clothing, and workload.

Reference: p. 329 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why should WBGT not be the sole method when impermeable clothing substantially limits evaporation?
Back:
The book states that NIOSH advises against using WBGT in that situation because evaporative cooling is restricted; heat-strain monitoring may be more feasible.

Example: Apply it when evaluating a hot-work task, clothing, and workload.

Reference: p. 329; pp. 333–335 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: HRR₁=105 bpm. How does it compare with the book’s 110-bpm criterion?
Back:
It is below the cited criterion of 110 bpm.

Example: Apply it when evaluating a hot-work task, clothing, and workload.

Reference: p. 342 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: At 90 dBA for 4 h plus 95 dBA for 2 h, what is OSHA mixed dose using the book’s table?
Back:
4/8 + 2/4 = 1.0, or 100% dose.

Example: Use it when evaluating workplace noise exposure or a hearing-conservation program.

Reference: p. 224 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: A worker is exposed to 100 dBA for 2 h and 110 dBA for 0.5 h. What is the OSHA mixed dose?
Back:
2/2 + 0.5/0.5 = 2.0, or 200% dose.

Example: Use it when evaluating workplace noise exposure or a hearing-conservation program.

Reference: p. 225 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why can octave-band analysis be more useful than a single dBA value when designing noise controls?
Back:
It identifies where noise energy lies across frequencies, which helps select appropriate engineering controls.

Example: Use it when evaluating workplace noise exposure or a hearing-conservation program.

Reference: p. 220 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: A sound level meter is used for an OSHA compliance measurement. Should it use fast or slow response?
Back:
Slow response.

Example: Use it when evaluating workplace noise exposure or a hearing-conservation program.

Reference: p. 220 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: With 0% impairment in one ear and 100% in the other, what binaural impairment does the book’s AMA example give?
Back:
17%: [(5×0%) + 100%]/6 = 16.7%, rounded to 17%.

Example: Use it when evaluating workplace noise exposure or a hearing-conservation program.

Reference: p. 96 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: A 100% binaural hearing impairment in the book's example translates to what whole-person impairment?
Back:
The example's 17% binaural impairment translates to 6% whole-person impairment.

Example: Use it when evaluating workplace noise exposure or a hearing-conservation program.

Reference: p. 96 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why is carbon monoxide classified as a chemical asphyxiant in the book?
Back:
It binds hemoglobin and interferes with oxygen transport rather than simply displacing oxygen.

Example: Use it to interpret how a hazardous agent may affect a worker after exposure.

Reference: p. 132 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why is methane a simple asphyxiant?
Back:
It can displace oxygen from the atmosphere, reducing the oxygen available for breathing.

Example: Use it to interpret how a hazardous agent may affect a worker after exposure.

Reference: p. 1001 (glossary) — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What does LD50 mean?
Back:
The dose expected to kill 50% of a defined experimental animal population, for routes other than inhalation.

Example: Use it to interpret how a hazardous agent may affect a worker after exposure.

Reference: p. 126 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What does LC50 mean?
Back:
The airborne concentration expected to kill 50% of a defined experimental animal population during a stated exposure period.

Example: Use it to interpret how a hazardous agent may affect a worker after exposure.

Reference: p. 127 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why must exposure duration accompany an LC value?
Back:
A given concentration can produce different effects depending on exposure duration, so the time period is integral to interpreting the LC.

Example: Use it to interpret how a hazardous agent may affect a worker after exposure.

Reference: p. 127 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: If motivation is the barrier, is training alone likely to change behavior?
Back:
No. The chapter states training can address lack of knowledge or incorrect knowledge, but not effectively a lack of motivation or attention.

Example: Apply it when planning, documenting, or evaluating an industrial hygiene program.

Front: Which IH step identifies potential hazards before work begins?
Back:
Anticipation.

Example: Review a new process before commissioning it.

Back:
Recognition.

Example: Identify solvent use during a walkthrough.

Front: Which IH step characterizes workers’ exposures to hazards?
Back:
Evaluation.

Example: Collect representative personal air samples.

Front: Which IH step reduces or removes workplace hazards?
Back:
Control.

Example: Enclose a process to prevent contaminant release.

Back:
Chemical hazards.

Back:
Physical hazards.

Ergonomic hazards.

Front: Which broad hazard category includes bacteria and viruses?
Back:
Biological hazards.

Example: A healthcare worker handles potentially infectious material.

Front: Which exposure route occurs when an agent enters through the skin?

Dermal absorption.

Example: A solvent contacts skin and passes through it.

Front: Which exposure route occurs when contaminated material is swallowed?
Back:
Ingestion.

Example: Contaminated hands transfer residue to food.

Front: Which IH program component defines policy and responsibilities?

Written policy and program.

Back:
Hazard recognition.

Hazard evaluation and exposure assessment.

Example: Sample workers in a similar exposure group.

Back:
Hazard control.

Employee training.

Employee involvement.

Back:

Front: How can pulmonary clearance affect response to the same inhaled exposure?
Back:

Front: How can smoking affect respiratory response to workplace exposure?

Back:
They can contribute to differences in metabolism or susceptibility.

Example: Two workers may respond differently to the same agent.

Back:
The middle ear.

Example: The ossicles transmit mechanical vibration.

Reference: p. 83 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which ear division contains the cochlea and sensory structures for hearing?
Back:
The inner ear.

Example: Cochlear hair cells convert vibration into neural signals.

Reference: p. 83 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which occupational exposure route involves breathing an airborne agent?
Back:
Inhalation.

Example: A worker breathes dust during bag dumping.

Reference: pp. 123–129 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which occupational exposure route involves agent contact with or passage through skin?
Back:
Dermal exposure.

Example: Liquid contaminant contacts an unprotected hand.

Reference: pp. 123–129 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which occupational exposure route involves swallowing an agent?
Back:
Ingestion.

Example: Residue transfers from contaminated fingers to the mouth.

Reference: pp. 123–129 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: How can higher solvent volatility affect airborne exposure potential?
Back:
It generally increases the tendency to enter the vapor phase.

Example: A volatile solvent can evaporate rapidly from an open tray.

Reference: pp. 149–165 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: How can higher temperature affect solvent vapor generation?
Back:
It generally increases evaporation and vapor concentration potential.

Example: Warm solvent may release vapor faster than cool solvent.

Reference: pp. 149–165 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: How can the work process affect solvent exposure?
Back:
Open handling, spraying, or agitation can change the rate and pattern of release.

Example: Spraying may generate both vapor and droplets.

Reference: pp. 149–165 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: How can ventilation affect solvent exposure?
Back:
Effective ventilation can capture or dilute released vapor.

Example: A properly designed hood captures vapor near a cleaning tank.

Reference: pp. 149–165 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: How can the amount of solvent used affect exposure?
Back:
A larger amount can increase the potential source term, depending on conditions.

Example: A large open bath can release more vapor than a small closed container.

Reference: pp. 149–165 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why does task duration matter for solvent exposure?
Back:
Longer exposure can increase the time-weighted average.

Example: A worker spends several hours cleaning parts with solvent.

Reference: pp. 149–165 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Why does the route of exposure matter for solvent risk?
Back:
Inhalation and skin contact can contribute differently to total uptake.

Example: Air sampling alone may not characterize substantial skin absorption.

Reference: pp. 149–165 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which fibrotic lung disease is associated with inhaled crystalline silica?
Back:
Silicosis.

Example: Respirable crystalline silica exposure can occur during concrete cutting.

Reference: pp. 180–205 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which fibrotic lung disease is associated with asbestos fibers?
Back:
Asbestosis.

Example: Disturbing asbestos-containing insulation can release fibers.

Reference: pp. 180–205 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which hearing-conservation element characterizes workers’ noise exposure?
Back:
Noise exposure monitoring.

Example: Measure representative exposures to determine who is covered.

Reference: p. 237 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which hearing-conservation element tracks hearing thresholds over time?
Back:
Audiometric testing.

Example: Compare a worker’s audiogram with the baseline.

Reference: p. 237 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which hearing-conservation element reduces sound reaching the ear?
Back:
Hearing protection.

Example: Select and fit suitable earplugs or earmuffs.

Reference: p. 237 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which hearing-conservation element explains risks and protective practices?
Back:
Employee training.

Example: Explain correct insertion of earplugs.

Reference: p. 237 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which hearing-conservation element preserves required program records?
Back:
Recordkeeping.

Example: Retain audiometric and exposure-monitoring records.

Reference: p. 237 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which ionizing radiation consists of helium nuclei?
Back:
Alpha particles.

Example: An alpha emitter is a concern if radioactive material is inhaled or ingested.

Reference: pp. 257–265 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which ionizing radiation consists of high-speed electrons or positrons?
Back:
Beta particles.

Example: Beta radiation can pose a skin or eye hazard.

Reference: pp. 257–265 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which ionizing radiation is high-energy electromagnetic radiation emitted by nuclei?
Back:
Gamma radiation.

Example: Gamma radiation may require shielding and distance controls.

Reference: pp. 257–265 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which ionizing radiation is high-energy electromagnetic radiation produced outside the nucleus?
Back:
X-rays.

Example: Industrial radiography uses X-rays to inspect welds.

Reference: pp. 257–265 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which ionizing radiation consists of uncharged particles from the nucleus?
Back:
Neutrons.

Example: Neutron exposure can occur near certain nuclear sources.

Reference: pp. 257–265 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which radiation-control method reduces exposure by limiting time near a source?
Back:
Time.

Example: Minimize time spent near an active source.

Reference: pp. 270–275 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which radiation-control method reduces exposure by increasing separation from a source?
Back:
Distance.

Example: Use remote handling tools to stand farther away.

Reference: pp. 270–275 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which radiation-control method reduces exposure by placing material between a person and source?
Back:
Shielding.

Example: Use shielding appropriate to the radiation type and energy.

Reference: pp. 270–275 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which nonionizing radiation band can cause photokeratitis?
Back:
Ultraviolet radiation.

Example: Arc welding can produce intense UV radiation.

Reference: pp. 281–325 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which nonionizing radiation band includes the light visible to the human eye?
Back:
Visible light.

Example: Intense visible light can create visual or retinal hazards.

Reference: pp. 281–325 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which nonionizing radiation band is associated with radiant heat?
Back:
Infrared radiation.

Example: Hot industrial surfaces emit infrared radiation.

Reference: pp. 281–325 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which nonionizing radiation uses coherent, highly directional optical energy?
Back:
Laser radiation.

Example: A laser alignment task may require wavelength-specific eye protection.

Reference: pp. 281–325 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which nonionizing radiation category includes radiofrequency and microwave fields?
Back:
Radiofrequency/microwave radiation.

Example: Assess exposure near RF heating equipment.

Reference: pp. 281–325 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which environmental factor group affects thermal stress?
Back:
Climatic conditions, including air temperature, humidity, air movement, and radiant heat.

Example: High humidity can limit evaporative cooling.

Reference: p. 328 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which worker/task factor affects thermal stress through internal heat production?
Back:
Work demands and metabolic rate.

Example: Heavy manual work generates more metabolic heat than seated work.

Reference: p. 328 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which personal/task factor can impede heat loss?
Back:
Clothing and personal protective equipment.

Example: Impermeable protective clothing can restrict evaporation.

Reference: p. 328 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which ergonomic risk factor involves exerting high muscular effort?
Back:
Force.

Example: Repeatedly gripping a heavy tool requires force.

Reference: pp. 399–414 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which ergonomic risk factor involves repeating the same movement frequently?
Back:
Repetition.

Example: Repeatedly fastening the same small component.

Reference: pp. 399–414 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which ergonomic risk factor involves holding joints away from neutral?
Back:
Awkward posture.

Example: Working for long periods with a bent wrist.

Reference: pp. 399–414 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which ergonomic risk factor involves sustained muscle loading without movement?
Back:
Static posture.

Example: Holding the arms elevated during overhead work.

Reference: pp. 399–414 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which ergonomic risk factor involves oscillatory mechanical energy transmitted to the body?
Back:
Vibration.

Example: Prolonged use of a vibrating hand tool.

Reference: pp. 399–414 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which ergonomic risk factor occurs when a hard edge presses into soft tissue?
Back:
Contact stress.

Example: The wrist rests against a sharp desk edge while typing.

Reference: pp. 399–414 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which biological hazard group includes single-celled prokaryotic organisms?
Back:
Bacteria.

Example: Certain bacteria can be present in contaminated water.

Reference: pp. 419–430 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which biological hazard group requires host cells to replicate?
Back:
Viruses.

Example: Blood or respiratory secretions may transmit viruses.

Reference: pp. 419–430 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which biological hazard group includes yeasts and molds?
Back:
Fungi.

Example: Damp building materials may support mold growth.

Reference: pp. 419–430 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which biological hazard group includes organisms such as protozoa and worms?
Back:
Parasites.

Example: Exposure may occur through contaminated water or biological material.

Reference: pp. 419–430 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is a biological toxin?
Back:
A harmful substance produced by a living organism.

Example: A toxin may cause illness even when the producing organism is not present.

Reference: pp. 419–430 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which biological exposure route involves inhaling airborne particles or droplets?
Back:
Inhalation.

Example: A worker inhales an aerosol generated during a procedure.

Reference: pp. 423–430 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which biological exposure route involves swallowing contaminated material?
Back:
Ingestion.

Example: Contaminated hands transfer material to the mouth.

Reference: pp. 423–430 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which biological exposure route involves contact with skin or mucous membranes?
Back:
Skin or mucous-membrane contact.

Example: Contaminated fluid splashes into the eye.

Reference: pp. 423–430 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which biological exposure route occurs when a contaminated sharp penetrates tissue?
Back:
Inoculation or percutaneous exposure.

Example: A needlestick introduces biological material through the skin.

Reference: pp. 423–430 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which air-sampling equipment provides an immediate reading without later laboratory analysis?
Back:
Direct-reading instruments.

Example: A direct-reading gas monitor displays concentration during a task.

Reference: p. 524 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which air-sampling equipment collects material for later laboratory analysis?
Back:
Sample-collection devices.

Example: A pump draws air through a filter cassette.

Reference: p. 524 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which particulate sampler collects particles on a porous medium?
Back:
A filter sampler.

Example: A pre-weighed filter collects airborne dust for gravimetric analysis.

Reference: pp. 527–531 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which particulate sampler separates particles by aerodynamic size using centrifugal action?
Back:
A cyclone.

Example: A cyclone selects a respirable fraction before a filter.

Reference: pp. 527–531 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which particulate collection device uses an electric field to collect charged particles?
Back:
An electrostatic precipitator.

Example: An electrostatic field drives particles onto a collection surface.

Reference: pp. 527–531 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which particulate collection device collects particles by inertial impaction?
Back:
An impactor.

Example: A cascade impactor separates aerosol by aerodynamic size.

Reference: pp. 527–531 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which particulate collection device captures particles in a liquid?
Back:
An impinger.

Example: Air bubbles through a collection liquid that retains the target material.

Reference: pp. 527–531 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which particulate separation device relies on differences in particle settling behavior?
Back:
An elutriator.

Example: Airflow and gravity separate particles of different aerodynamic sizes.

Reference: pp. 527–531 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which engineering-control strategy replaces a hazard with a less hazardous option?
Back:
Substitution.

Example: Replace a high-volatility solvent with a suitable lower-volatility alternative.

Reference: p. 594 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which engineering-control strategy separates people from the hazard?
Back:
Isolation.

Example: Operate a noisy process in a separate room.

Reference: p. 594 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which engineering-control strategy physically contains a hazard or release?
Back:
Enclosure.

Example: Enclose a dusty transfer point.

Reference: p. 594 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which engineering-control strategy captures or removes contaminants from air?
Back:
Ventilation.

Example: Use local exhaust to capture welding fume.

Reference: p. 594 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which local exhaust component captures contaminant near its source?
Back:
The hood.

Example: A hood is positioned near a welding arc.

Reference: p. 595 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which local exhaust component conveys contaminated air?
Back:
The ductwork.

Example: Ducts transport captured fume toward the air cleaner or fan.

Reference: p. 595 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which local exhaust component removes contaminants from the airstream when needed?
Back:
The air cleaner.

Example: A suitable collector removes particulate before discharge.

Reference: p. 595 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which local exhaust component supplies the pressure difference that moves air?
Back:
The fan.

Example: A fan maintains the required system airflow.

Reference: p. 595 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which local exhaust component releases treated or exhausted air at a discharge point?
Back:
The stack or discharge.

Example: A properly designed stack disperses exhaust away from air intakes.

Reference: p. 595 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What does workplace characterization document in an exposure assessment?
Back:
Processes, tasks, materials, controls, and conditions where work occurs.

Example: Map when and where a powder is transferred.

Reference: pp. 795–796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What does workforce characterization document in an exposure assessment?
Back:
Worker groups, tasks, schedules, and work patterns relevant to exposure.

Example: Identify employees who perform the same cleaning task.

Reference: pp. 795–796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What does agent characterization document in an exposure assessment?
Back:
The hazardous agent’s properties, health effects, and relevant exposure criteria.

Example: Identify the chemical and its applicable exposure limit.

Reference: pp. 795–796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the purpose of an audit opening conference?
Back:
Explain the audit scope, process, and expectations.

Example: Confirm the areas and records that will be reviewed.

Reference: p. 800 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What happens during audit information gathering?
Back:
Relevant documents, observations, and interviews are collected.

Example: Review sampling reports and observe a work task.

Reference: p. 800 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What happens during audit analysis and confirmation?
Back:
Evidence is checked and potential findings are validated.

Example: Confirm a reported control failure with direct observation.

Reference: p. 800 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the purpose of an audit closing conference?
Back:
Communicate preliminary findings and clarify factual issues.

Example: Review findings with responsible site personnel.

Reference: p. 800 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is the purpose of the audit report?
Back:
Document findings, supporting evidence, and recommended corrective actions.

Example: Record an assigned action and due date for each finding.

Reference: p. 800 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What averaging period does a TLV-TWA use for the conventional work schedule?
Back:
A conventional 8-hour workday and 40-hour workweek.

Example: Compare an 8-hour TWA result with the applicable TLV-TWA.

Reference: pp. 24, 919+ — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What averaging period defines a TLV-STEL?
Back:
A 15-minute time-weighted average that should not be exceeded, subject to the substance’s guidance.

Example: Evaluate a 15-minute task sample against the TLV-STEL when one is established.

Reference: pp. 24, 919+ — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What does a TLV-C limit?
Back:
A concentration that should not be exceeded during any part of the working exposure.

Example: Evaluate brief high-concentration events against the applicable ceiling value.

Reference: pp. 24, 919+ — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is sampling-method error?
Back:
Random variability introduced by the sampling procedure or equipment.

Example: Small differences in collection efficiency can change sample results.

Reference: p. 997 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is analytical-method error?
Back:
Random variability introduced during laboratory measurement and analysis.

Example: Replicate analyses of the same sample produce slightly different results.

Reference: p. 997 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: What is environmental variability?
Back:
Real changes in exposure conditions over time or between circumstances.

Example: Dust concentration changes as production rate changes.

Reference: p. 997 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which exposure-assessment characterization describes the process and physical setting?
Back:
Workplace characterization.

Example: Document process steps, materials, and controls.

Reference: pp. 795–796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which exposure-assessment characterization describes the people and work patterns?
Back:
Workforce characterization.

Example: Group workers by similar tasks and schedules.

Reference: pp. 795–796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).

Front: Which exposure-assessment characterization describes the hazardous agent?
Back:
Agent characterization.

Example: Identify the agent’s health effects and exposure criteria.

Reference: pp. 795–796 — Fundamentals of Industrial Hygiene, 5th ed. (2002).
